root_cause: attempt_direct_s0_write's failed INSERT (readonly connection) left an implicit sqlite3 read transaction open (python legacy transaction handling begins a BEGIN before any DML, even one that then raises); without an explicit rollback, the connection stayed pinned to its pre-attempt snapshot and stopped observing later committed writes on that object_key.
fix: self.s0.rollback() added in the caught OperationalError branch of attempt_direct_s0_write, tools/zero_entityos_restart_resize_db_smoke_v1.py
regression_check: targeted tests/ sweep: 98 failed/1302 passed before -> 97 failed/1304 passed after; one pre-existing failure fixed (the smoke test itself), zero new regressions, same 97 unrelated pre-existing failures

hypothesis_and_implications.hypothesis: This is a generic Python sqlite3 gotcha (legacy isolation_level='' begins implicit transactions before DML, not before SELECT), not specific to this project's design -- it likely would have surfaced in ANY future read-only-connection test that calls a rejected-write probe before doing epoch-sensitive reads on the same connection.
hypothesis_and_implications.implication_for_grid10: Gabriel's planned physical GRID10 work depends on solid S0 epoch/CAS guarantees under concurrent load. This exact bug pattern (a caught exception on a DML statement silently leaving an open read transaction) is worth grepping for elsewhere in the S0/S1 write-path code before trusting other CAS-adjacent modules under real concurrency -- this fork did not do that broader sweep, scope was limited to the one proven blocker per the fail-closed rule.
hypothesis_and_implications.implication_for_read_only_connections: Any code opening a sqlite3 connection with mode=ro and then deliberately probing it with a write attempt (as a boundary-enforcement test) must rollback after the expected failure, or risk silently stale reads for the connection's entire remaining lifetime -- this is easy to miss because the immediate assertion (write was rejected) still passes; only a LATER read reveals the staleness.
